title: Physicists Aim to Test Matter and Antimatter Symmetry Using Molecular
excerpt: Physicists from Germany and the United Kingdom have secured European Research Council funding to synthesize, transport, and measure antihydrogen molecular ions using precision laser spectroscopy.
content:
A collaborative research team of German and United Kingdom physicists from Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Leibniz University Hannover, and Swansea University in Wales has initiated a project to examine whether minuscule physical differences exist between matter and antimatter. The project, titled Extending the Horizons of Precision Antimatter Spectroscopy, aims to produce antihydrogen molecular ions, transport them between facilities, and analyze them with laser and radiation sources. Supported by a fourteen million euro Synergy Grant from the European Research Council distributed over six years, the collaboration intends to achieve measurement accuracies several orders of magnitude beyond those reached in previous antimatter experiments, with Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf receiving approximately six point eight million euros of the total funding allocation.

According to established physical theory, matter and antimatter were generated in equal quantities during the Big Bang, with particles and their corresponding antiparticles expected to share identical masses, lifetimes, and interactions while differing only in their positive or negative electric charges and magnetic moments. Because particles and antiparticles annihilate upon physical contact, the observed predominance of matter in the modern universe presents an unresolved problem for fundamental physics. Professor Stefan Ulmer, who holds the Chair of Quantum Technologies and Fundamental Symmetries at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf and serves as coordinating principal investigator for the initiative, explained that the observable prevalence of matter could reflect an undiscovered asymmetry between matter and antimatter that permitted a net residual quantity of matter to endure after the Big Bang.

To investigate this potential discrepancy, the research team has selected comparative laser spectroscopy of molecular systems. Professor Stephan Schiller, holder of the Chair of Quantum Optics at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf and a principal investigator on the project, noted that detecting even minor spectral deviations between corresponding systems would provide empirical evidence of a fundamental divergence between matter and antimatter. However, earlier experimental evaluations of atoms, atomic nuclei, and electrons have constrained any possible differences to exceptionally small scales. Consequently, existing experimental tools must be refined to expand the sensitivity of comparative precision measurements.

In evaluating experimental approaches, the researchers assessed comparative spectroscopy across several candidate systems, including antiprotons, antihydrogen atoms, and antiprotonic helium. Each of these options presented theoretical or experimental constraints that have prevented researchers from narrowing the achievable frequency deviation accuracy below one part in a trillion, representing a relative precision threshold of ten to the power of minus twelve. To surpass this limitation, the physicists selected the molecular ion of antihydrogen, designated as H̄2-, which comprises two antiprotons bound by a single positron, as the primary subject of investigation.

The antihydrogen molecular ion is regarded as an optimal experimental candidate because it is suitable for optical spectroscopy and exhibits an inherently narrow spectral linewidth, a property that facilitates ultra-precise measurement. Professor Schiller and his research team at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf previously attained a spectral resolution of ten to the power of minus twelve during spectroscopy of standard hydrogen molecular ions using technology developed in Düsseldorf. That demonstrated capability provides the baseline methodology and instrumental foundation for the planned spectroscopic evaluations of the corresponding antimatter ion.

Implementing the experimental program requires the collaboration to address multiple technical challenges across distinct scientific institutions. The initial stage involves the synthesis of the antihydrogen molecular ions, a process overseen by Professor Stefan Eriksson from Swansea University, who participates in the ALPHA collaboration at the European Organization for Nuclear Research, known as CERN, located in Geneva. CERN is currently the only facility globally with the infrastructure capable of producing these antimatter molecular ions. Professor Eriksson emphasized that synthesizing antimatter molecular ions demands advanced production techniques and that the initial synthesis rate is expected to remain low, necessitating numerous experimental trials and rigorous containment protocols to trap and preserve every produced anti-molecule without loss during handling.

Following synthesis at CERN, the ions cannot undergo final high-precision spectroscopy on site because magnetic field fluctuations generated by the facility’s multiple particle accelerators restrict the achievable measurement precision. Consequently, the research plan requires transporting the antihydrogen molecular ions to dedicated laboratories at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf. In March 2026, the BASE collaboration, directed by Professor Ulmer, demonstrated the feasibility of transporting antimatter particles using a mobile containment device known as the BASE-STEP mobile trap. While the BASE-STEP apparatus can theoretically hold and move antihydrogen molecular ions, researchers must implement further engineering developments to adapt the trap for long-distance transport between Geneva and Düsseldorf.

Once the antihydrogen molecular ions arrive at the specialized Düsseldorf facility, researchers will conduct laser spectroscopy and compare the measured transition frequencies with data obtained from matter molecular ions. Professor Christian Ospelkaus of Leibniz University Hannover, working in coordination with the National Metrology Institute of Germany, also known as the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt in Braunschweig, is contributing quantum-limited measurement techniques designed to meet the target precision criteria. The comparative spectroscopic analyses are scheduled to conclude by 2032, at which point the experimental results will determine whether matter and antimatter exhibit measurable differences within the achieved experimental sensitivity, an outcome that Professor Ospelkaus noted would indicate physical phenomena extending beyond existing theoretical models.

The European Research Council awarded the Synergy Grant to the project, formally designated as Extending the Horizons of Precision Antimatter Spectroscopy, or EHPAS. This funding mechanism supports collaborative research that combines distinct areas of expertise to achieve goals that individual groups might not reach alone. The total grant amount is fourteen million euros, distributed over a six-year period. Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf will receive approximately six point eight million euros of this total sum. The remaining funds support the partner institutions, including Leibniz University Hannover and Swansea University. The grant structure reflects the interdisciplinary nature of the work, which spans quantum optics, fundamental symmetries, and antimatter production. By pooling resources and specialized knowledge, the team aims to overcome the technical barriers that have previously limited the precision of antimatter measurements. The financial support enables the development of new instrumentation and the execution of long-term experimental campaigns necessary for high-accuracy spectroscopy.

Professor Stefan Ulmer, the coordinating principal investigator, holds the Chair of Quantum Technologies and Fundamental Symmetries at the Institute for Experimental Physics at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf. His role involves overseeing the overall scientific strategy and ensuring that the various components of the project align with the primary objective of testing matter-antimatter symmetry. Professor Stephan Schiller, who holds the Chair of Quantum Optics at the same institute, serves as the second principal investigator. His expertise in laser spectroscopy is central to the proposed method of comparing matter and antimatter. The collaboration also includes Professor Dr Christian Ospelkaus from Leibniz University Hannover, who leads the group contributing quantum-limited measurement methods. Professor Dr Stefan Eriksson from Swansea University is responsible for the production of the antimatter molecules. This distribution of responsibilities ensures that each critical aspect of the experimental pipeline is managed by specialists in their respective fields.

The theoretical motivation for the project stems from the unresolved question of why the universe is predominantly composed of matter. According to standard cosmological models, the Big Bang should have produced equal amounts of matter and antimatter. This asymmetry allowed a tiny excess of matter to survive the annihilation process. The EHPAS project seeks to identify whether this asymmetry arises from a fundamental difference in the properties of matter and antimatter that has not yet been detected. Finding such a difference would provide a crucial clue to understanding the origin of the matter-dominated cosmos.

Previous experiments have already placed strict constraints on any potential differences between matter and antimatter. Measurements of atoms, atomic nuclei, and electrons have shown that any deviations must be extremely small. The current state of the art in antimatter spectroscopy has achieved a precision of one part in a trillion, or ten to the power of minus twelve. The team believes that by moving to molecular systems, specifically the antihydrogen molecular ion, they can push the precision limits further.

The choice of the antihydrogen molecular ion, H̄2-, is based on its favorable properties for high-precision spectroscopy. The ion consists of two antiprotons and one positron. The expected linewidth of the spectral transitions is very narrow, which is ideal for detecting minute shifts in frequency. Professor Schiller’s team has already demonstrated the capability to achieve a resolution of ten to the power of minus twelve in the spectroscopy of regular hydrogen molecular ions. This prior success provides a strong foundation for the proposed antimatter experiments. The technology developed in Düsseldorf for hydrogen molecular ions will be adapted for use with the antimatter counterpart.

The production of antihydrogen molecular ions is a complex process that requires advanced synthesis techniques. Professor Eriksson’s team at Swansea University, in collaboration with the ALPHA collaboration at CERN, will be responsible for generating these ions. CERN is currently the only facility in the world capable of producing antimatter molecules. The production rate is expected to be low initially, meaning that the team will need to conduct many trials to accumulate enough data for precise measurements. This low production rate necessitates highly efficient trapping and storage systems. The team must ensure that every single anti-molecule produced is captured and preserved without loss. The development of robust containment protocols is therefore a critical component of the project.

Transporting the antihydrogen molecular ions from CERN to Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf presents another significant technical challenge. The magnetic field fluctuations at CERN, caused by the operation of multiple particle accelerators, limit the achievable precision of on-site measurements. To overcome this limitation, the ions must be moved to a quieter magnetic environment at the Düsseldorf laboratory. In March 2026, the BASE collaboration, led by Professor Ulmer, successfully demonstrated the transport of antimatter particles using the BASE-STEP mobile trap. However, the BASE-STEP trap requires further development to accommodate the specific needs of transporting antihydrogen molecular ions. The engineering modifications will ensure that the ions remain stable and confined during the journey. This transport capability is essential for accessing the high-precision measurement environment at HHU.

Upon arrival at the Düsseldorf laboratory, the antihydrogen molecular ions will undergo laser spectroscopy. The research group led by Professor Ospelkaus will employ quantum-limited measurement methods to achieve the target precision. The comparison between the spectra of matter and antimatter molecular ions will be the final step in the experimental process. If any differences are observed, they would indicate a violation of matter-antimatter symmetry. The results of these comparisons are scheduled to be completed by 2032. The outcome will determine whether the current theoretical models need to be revised or if the symmetry between matter and antimatter holds at the level of precision achieved.
